# Approximate Training
:label:`sec_approx_train`

Fortunately, since $L(w_o)-1$ is on the order of $\mathcal{O}(\text{log}_2|\mathcal{V}|)$ due to the binary tree structure,
when the dictionary size $\mathcal{V}$ is huge,
the computational cost for  each training step using hierarchical softmax
is significantly reduced compared with that
without approximate training.

In order to reduce the aforementioned computational complexity, this section will introduce two approximate training methods:
*negative sampling* and *hierarchical softmax*.

Due to the similarity
between the skip-gram model and
the continuous bag of words model,
we will just take the skip-gram model as an example
to describe these two approximate training methods.

Now that we know the technical details of 
the word2vec models and approximate training methods,
let us walk through their implementations.
We use negative sampling for approximate training.

![Hierarchical softmax for approximate training, where each leaf node of the tree represents a word in the dictionary.](../img/hi-softmax.svg)
:label:`fig_hi_softmax`
[Synthetic] Approximate training cuts computation, whereas exact training evaluates the full objective each step.

evidence_contexts.source_text: One of the key features of a bidirectional RNN is that information from both ends of the sequence is used to estimate the output.

As a specific example
illustrated in :numref:`fig_nlp-map-sa-rnn`,
we will represent each token
using the pretrained GloVe model,
and feed these token representations
into a multilayer bidirectional RNN
to obtain the text sequence representation,
which will
be transformed into 
sentiment analysis outputs :cite:`Maas.Daly.Pham.ea.2011`.
:numref:`fig_birnn` illustrates the architecture of a bidirectional RNN with a single hidden layer.
Bidirectional RNNs were introduced by :cite:`Schuster.Paliwal.1997`.
Hence, if we were to use a bidirectional RNN naively we would not get a very good accuracy: during training we have past and future data to estimate the present.
*Bidirectional RNNs* add a hidden layer that passes information in a backward direction to more flexibly process such information.

In deep bidirectional RNNs with multiple hidden layers,
such information
is passed on as *input* to the next bidirectional layer.

![Architecture of a bidirectional RNN.](../img/birnn.svg)
:label:`fig_birnn`
Synthetic: A bidirectional RNN reads the sequence in both directions, unlike a unidirectional RNN.

source_payload.proposed_definition_en: a recurrent neural network architecture that processes a sequence in both forward and backward directions
